title: Wrap the Axon, Make the Signal Jump

scenes.tts: How does a nerve signal travel fast down a thin axon? Think of a bare axon as a leaky garden hose. Current leaks out across its membrane at every point. So the action potential has to be rebuilt on every patch it reaches. That is slow. Patch after patch, the signal creeps.
scenes.visual: A long bare axon; a pulse is rebuilt patch by patch with leak arrows; a question mark asks how to go faster.
scenes.narration: How does a nerve signal travel fast down a thin axon? Think of a bare axon as a leaky garden hose. Current leaks out across its membrane at every point. So the action potential has to be rebuilt on every patch it reaches. That is slow. Patch after patch, the signal creeps.

scenes.tts: The answer is to wrap it. The wrapping is called myelin. Myelin is membrane from a glial cell. In the brain, that cell is an oligodendrocyte. In a nerve, it is a Schwann cell. The cell winds its membrane many times around the axon. The turns are squeezed until almost no cytoplasm is left between them.
scenes.visual: Axon cross-section; a glial sheet winds around it in a growing spiral; layers are then squeezed tight.
scenes.narration: The answer is to wrap it. The wrapping is called myelin. Myelin is membrane from a glial cell. In the brain, that cell is an oligodendrocyte. In a nerve, it is a Schwann cell. The cell winds its membrane many times around the axon. The turns are squeezed until almost no cytoplasm is left between them.

scenes.tts: Think of many thin walls stacked in a row. Together they make leaking much harder. Membranes stacked in series raise the resistance across the axon's wall. They also lower its capacitance. So current entering at one spot travels farther. And it charges the membrane ahead faster.

scenes.visual: Side by side: bare axon with big leak arrows and short current reach, wrapped axon with no leaks and a long current arrow.
scenes.narration: Think of many thin walls stacked in a row. Together they make leaking much harder. Membranes stacked in series raise the resistance across the axon's wall. They also lower its capacitance. So current entering at one spot travels farther. And it charges the membrane ahead faster.

scenes.tts: The wrap is not continuous. Short gaps lie between the sheaths. These gaps are the nodes of Ron vee ay. Each node is a short stretch of bare axon. Each wrapped stretch is an internode. The axon packs its voltage-gated sodium channels into the nodes. They sit there, and not under the sheath.

scenes.visual: Axon with sheaths and gaps; gaps labelled node, stretches labelled internode; sodium channels appear only at the nodes.

scenes.tts: Now follow the signal along the wrapped axon. The action potential is regenerated only at the nodes. Between nodes, current spreads quietly under the insulation. It reaches the next node. There the signal is rebuilt again. So the signal seems to leap from one node to the next. This is saltatory conduction, from the Latin for to jump.
scenes.visual: A flash at node one, current arrow under the sheath, flash at node two, and so on along the axon.
scenes.narration: Now follow the signal along the wrapped axon. The action potential is regenerated only at the nodes. Between nodes, current spreads quietly under the insulation. It reaches the next node. There the signal is rebuilt again. So the signal seems to leap from one node to the next. This is saltatory conduction, from the Latin for to jump.

scenes.tts: The gain is large. In a bare axon, speed rises with the square root of diameter. In a myelinated fiber, speed rises in proportion to diameter. The largest mammalian fibers reach tens of meters per second. A classic estimate is about six meters per second for each micrometer. Thin bare fibers conduct at about one meter per second or less. Wrap the axon, and the signal jumps from gap to gap.
scenes.visual: Plot of speed against diameter: a flattening curve for bare axons, a straight rising line for myelinated fibers, a marker for the thin bare fiber.
